terms.definition: A test function decorated with `@scenario(...)`. Not every pytest test is a scenario — undecorated tests are tolerated but not collected.

The text `@scenario` takes first: the statement of the rule a *Scenario* demonstrates, shown as its heading in the report. A plain string, a t-string of glossary handles, or a `Template` filled per *Case*; recorded as the scenario's *Narration*. Not the test function's name, which the node ID carries.

A unit of narration: a `with given(...)` / `when(...)` / `then(...)` block, or the root recording from a step fixture. Steps nest, and each carries a phase, narration, attachments and children — but no status or error of its own: a failure is recorded on the *Scenario*, and per *Case* on the *Parameter table*.

The human-readable text on a step or scenario title. A `Narration` bundles the flat rendered `text` with `parts` — empty for plain-string authoring, and for a t-string or `pytest_given.Template` a list of `NarrationLiteral` / `NarrationValue` / `NarrationPlaceholder` / `NarrationTermRef` pieces.
The category of a step: `given`, `when`, or `then`. A step has exactly one phase.

A step-authoring helper that emits a `when` action and its `then` outcome as two sibling steps from a single `with` block. Used mainly to narrate an expected raise (`with when_then('the action', 'the error is raised'), pytest.raises(...)`), so the action and its outcome stay distinct steps.
Free-form string label attached via `@scenario(title, tags=[...])`. A `/` nests it: `ticket/ABC-123` sits under `ticket`.
A labeled blob (text or JSON) bound to the currently-active step via `attach(label, content)`.
A `@scenario`-decorated test that also carries `@pytest.mark.parametrize(...)`. Produces multiple scenario records during a run; pytest-given groups them.
One row of a parametrized scenario — its node ID, a single tuple of parameter values, its status, and any error.

A *Case*'s pytest ID: its *Node ID*'s parametrize tail without the brackets (`touching-edges`), as the terminal prints it. *Custom* when it is more than its values' generated parts, as from `pytest.param(..., id=...)` or `ids=`.

The per-scenario grouping of typed columns + cases. A column is a `param` (a `@pytest.mark.parametrize` input), a `derived` (a narrated value that varies across cases) or an `attachment` (an attachment whose payload varies).

Collapsing the N scenario records of a parametrized scenario into one logical scenario carrying a *Parameter table*. Cases group when they share both the same name and the same *Node ID* without its parametrize tail — one test function; two same-named scenarios on different test functions stay separate. `@scenario(group_parametrized=False)` declines the merge, so each case lives on as its own scenario.

Derive the grouped-template step text by comparing every comparable case: what all of them share stays inline, and anything that varies becomes a `{name}` placeholder or attachment badge pointing at a parameter-table column. The baseline tree comes from the first passed case, and every other passed case must narrate that same template.
A pytest fixture whose function is wrapped with `@given(text)`. Only `@given` is allowed on fixtures; `@when` / `@then` are rejected.
A pytest fixture without a pytest-given decorator. It produces no step in the report unless a *Given annotation* on the test's parameter narrates it.

A `given(...)` in a test parameter's `Annotated[...]` type: `def test(room: Annotated[int, given('a room')])`. On a parametrize value or a *Plain fixture* it adds a childless `given` step; on a *Step fixture* it replaces the fixture's root label and its pins. Only `given` is allowed, and a `Template` in it may only hold a bare parametrize column.
A captured subtree of steps + attachments produced while a step fixture is being set up. A generator fixture's teardown records nothing — it refuses steps and attachments.
Attaching a fixture recording into the active scenario's step tree at the moment its host test starts.
The per-session object accumulating scenarios, fixture recordings, and parameter info.
The scenario currently being recorded into.
A pytest test identifier (e.g., `tests/test_x.py::test_y[a-b]`).
The chain of currently-open steps. A `with given(...)` pushes one, and leaving the block pops it.
The output artifact: a JSON data file and optional self-contained HTML and Markdown renderings derived from it. The JSON is the source of truth.
Converts a JSON report into a rendering — a self-contained HTML page or a Markdown document.
Each parametrize column gets a stable highlight color; placeholders and matching values share that color wherever they appear in step text and the parameter table.

A neutral highlight applied to t-string interpolation values that don't correspond to a parametrize column and are constant across every case (e.g., a computed expression like `price * 1.2`). One that varies becomes a `derived` column instead.
A clickable file:line anchor on a scenario card, a story panel, or an expanded glossary term card. It points at a scenario's test function, or at the declaration of a *Story* or *Term*.

A Markdown link to a scenario, tag or story in the HTML *Report*: the report's URL with a `#scenario=<node ID>`, `#tag=<tag>` or `#view=stories&story=<story id>` fragment. Without a glyph it is a plain one, which claims only that its target exists.

A *Report link* led by its target's status glyph, citing a scenario, tag or story from a Markdown document: `✅ [title](<report URL>#scenario=…)`. A tag or story citation adds a summary after it, `(5 ✅ · 2 🔵)`. A target the *Report* lacks reads `❓`.
A *Citation* of a scenario written as a `<details markdown="1">` block, the citation in its `<summary>` and the scenario's Markdown narration in its body.
One problem `pytest-given citations check` reports on one *Report link*: its kind (`stale`, `missing`, `failed`, `mistyped`, …), the document location and a message.
The HTML report's colour scheme — `light`, `dark`, or `auto` (follow the viewer's system).

The `--given-lint` pass that checks recorded scenarios against the *Lint rule* catalog. It enforces the structural subset of the narration conventions — it cannot check whether a *Step*'s text is semantically true.
One named check, carrying a surface and a default *Severity*. A `runtime` rule reads the recorded scenarios; an `ast` rule parses the step bodies' source.
One *Lint rule* firing on one subject: the rule id, the *Severity* it fired at, the subject, a *Source link* location and a message naming the offender.
A *Lint rule*'s level — `off`, `warn` or `error`. Only `error` fails the run, `warn` reports in the terminal summary, and an `off` rule is not evaluated at all.
The Ubiquitous-Language concept — the shared vocabulary a domain speaks in — and the class that realizes it in code: `Glossary()`, on which terms are registered.
A glossary loaded from the GFM pipe tables of a Markdown file, via the `FileGlossary(path)` class.

A term handed over before its kind is settled — what `g('foo')` and `g['foo']` on a code glossary return, and every *file glossary* lookup. The handle is the same `TermHandle` the typed registrations (`g.actor(...)` and friends) hand back; `declared_kind is None` is what marks the deferral. The deferral is in the handing over, not the term: a row with an explicit `kind_column` arrives through the same handle already kinded, while the rest stay `None` until *kind inference* runs.
A registered glossary entry: an Actor, Work Object, Activity, or kindless term. Each carries an id (slug), a canonical name, a kind (`None` when kindless), and an optional definition.

The Python object a glossary hands back for a *term* — `TermHandle`, the same type from every accessor (`g.actor(...)`, `g('foo')`, `g['Guest']`, a captured `guest = ...`). It is what steps, scenario titles and sentences interpolate, in one of four surface forms: **bare** (`room` — the canonical display), **`.l`** (`room.l` — capitalized words lowercased, acronyms kept), **`.s`** (`room.s` — the *S-form*), or **called** (`room('Deluxe Suite')` — an *instance* on an Actor or Work Object, an inflection on an *Activity*). `.l` and `.s` also apply to a called form and chain (`room.l.s` reads *rooms*). Each form renders as a *term ref*. A story hands out a **sentence handle** the same way: `book_a_room['cancel']` by name or `book_a_room[3]` by number, which `pins=` takes.

A term's name with the regular English -s ending, from the `.s` handle form: the plural of an Actor or Work Object (*rooms*), the third person singular of an Activity (*books*). It adds -s to the last word, -es after s, x, z, ch or sh, and turns a consonant + y into -ies, but an acronym takes a plain -s (*APIs*); anything else, such as *people* or *checks in*, needs the called form. An S-form reference, in any case, is a reference to the term itself — not an *instance* or an *inflection*.
A glossary term for a participant in the domain (e.g., *Guest*).
A glossary term for a thing acted on (e.g., *Room*, *Booking*).

A glossary term for what an actor does (e.g., *book*, *confirm*), which Domain Storytelling draws as an arrow labelled with a verb. Activities accept inflections: calling `search('searches for')` records *searches for* as a surface form of the canonical *search*.
An occurrence of a term inside narration. Modeled as `NarrationTermRef` in step text and as `ClauseTermRef` inside a clause.
A named refinement of an Actor or Work Object (e.g., `guest('Alice')` is an instance of the *Guest* actor).
A surface form of an Activity term other than its canonical name or *S-form* (e.g., *searches for* as an inflection of *search*).
A named flow modeled as a sequence of sentences. Constructed by `story('Title', [sentence(...), ...])`. Stories are the unit of coverage.

What Domain Storytelling calls a sentence: an actor, an activity and its work objects, plus connective words. One row in a story, numbered by its position (1..N, never set by hand) and optionally named with `sentence(..., name='cancel')`, a name that stays put when rows are inserted. Constructed by `sentence(...)`. Usually one clause, built implicitly; several when the sentence has several arrows under one number.

The two-variant union making up a clause's prose (`ClausePart` = `ClauseTermRef` or `ClauseWord`): a reference to a glossary term, whose kind resolves via the glossary, or a bare clause word — a node label or edge connective that carries no kind or id, is never classified by inference, and never reaches the glossary. That last is what separates it from a kindless term, which has an id and is tracked.

One linear walk through a sentence's arrows, a node/edge alternation starting actor → verb → noun, constructed by `clause(...)`. A sentence with several arrow chains under one number, such as an actor handing a work object to two recipients, takes one clause per chain. Domain Storytelling names no such unit.
A position role in a clause, from its node/edge alternation: position 0 is the actor slot, odd positions are verb slots, and even positions ≥ 2 are noun slots.

The link between a scenario (or step) and story sentences. `@scenario(stories=...)` names the stories a scenario is narration-matched against; a *pin* (`pins=` on `@scenario` or on `given`/`when`/`then`) binds sentences explicitly, in any story, whether `stories=` names it or not.

What a *sentence handle* passed to `pins=` is recorded as, the way a term handle in narration is recorded as a *term ref*: a `Pin` naming a story and a sentence number. A pin binds explicitly and replaces narration matching — a step pin for that step, a scenario pin (`@scenario(pins=...)`) for every step of the scenario, which then covers its own pins plus its steps'. `pins=[]` pins nothing but still opts out of narration matching. A pin reaches under-anchored sentences too.

The "did this scenario touch that sentence" relation. Computed by the *A_refs ⊆ S* rule: a sentence is covered when the set of terms it references is a subset of the terms a single step references — matching is per step, not against the union across steps, and on terms, not surface forms: an *instance* or *inflection* counts as its term. A *pin* covers its sentences directly instead, regardless of narration or term count.

The post-collection pass (`infer_glossary_kinds`) that assigns each undeclared term a kind from the *slot* positions it occupies across all story sentences; declared kinds are verified against observed positions instead. A term used in incompatible slots (or conflicting with its declared kind) raises. A term never referenced by any sentence stays *kindless*.
A term with `kind=None` — left unset when *kind inference* finds no story *slot* to infer from (a term used only in t-string steps, never in a sentence).
A term with `definition is None`. Orthogonal to *kindless*.
Person who writes the application code and — together with the *Agent* — the scenarios; curates the glossary with the *Domain Expert*.
Person who owns the domain knowledge and the ubiquitous language; source of domain stories and reviewer of scenarios and reports. A stakeholder in the broad sense.
AI coding agent that authors and maintains scenarios alongside the *Developer*, guided by the pytest-given skills.
